title: Unit Testing SQL Logic
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of unit testing sql logic.
Apply testing expected results in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn unit testing sql logic through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Unit Testing SQL Logic matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Professional work with unit testing sql logic means that another person can review, repeat, and safely operate the query. Keep formatting consistent, test meaningful edge cases, use versioned migrations, and document engine/version assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Testing expected results, Testing empty input, Testing NULL values, Testing duplicate records. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Testing expected results
items.text: Testing expected results helps break a larger query into a precise question. Check the subquery's row count and output columns, account for NULLs in membership tests, and compare the result with a simpler equivalent on a small dataset.

items.title: Testing empty input
items.text: Testing empty input makes SQL easier to change safely. Turn assumptions into repeatable checks, keep schema/query changes reviewable, use deterministic ordering, and record the data shape and environment used for the check.

items.title: Testing NULL values
items.text: Testing NULL values requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

items.title: Testing duplicate records
items.text: Testing duplicate records makes SQL easier to change safely. Turn assumptions into repeatable checks, keep schema/query changes reviewable, use deterministic ordering, and record the data shape and environment used for the check.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count, COALESCE(SUM(total_amount), 0) AS total_amount
FROM orders;
content_blocks.expected_output: The result reports the number of orders and a total amount, using zero for an empty sum only for display.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate unit testing sql logic using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic testing expected results and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Unit Testing SQL Logic is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
